Reviewing the current evidence: headline CPI has decelerated from its recent high of 2.85% to 2.64%, a 0.21 pp drop. This is meaningful but modest. Core PCE stands at 2.00%, exactly at the Fed's 2% target for the first time in this series. The 3-month annualized headline rate is 1.40%—well below the current YoY level—suggesting underlying momentum has cooled. The month-to-month reading (0.18%) is above the 3-month average (0.12%), indicating the most recent print picked up slightly. Headline is still elevated within its 12-month range, at the 75th percentile position (0.62 pp above the low of 2.02%).

The divergence between headline and core has widened to -0.65 pp, with core now holding the 2% target while headline remains above it. This suggests energy/food volatility is the primary driver of headline elevation, not persistent demand-side pressure.

The falsifier I set—m/m prints above 0.25%—was not breached; the recent 0.18% fell short. Core PCE at 2.00% did not fall below 1.85%, so that condition was not met either. However, my prior conviction was already modest (0.48), and the actual outcome (mild decline rather than more substantial deceleration) warrants recalibration downward. The evidence now points to continued deceleration in the near term, but at a slower pace than my previous view implied.

For the next month-ahead release, headline CPI is more likely to remain flat or move modestly lower, as the 3m annualized pace is structurally slower than the current YoY level, and core is now at target. Conviction should be moderate, not high, because momentum has slowed but recent prints show volatility.

The most recent headline CPI reading of 1.88% y/y is still below the threshold I specified; momentum has not stabilized sustainably above +0.15% either. The three-month annualized headline rate sits at +2.41%, but this reflects the volatile +0.38% m/m print at the outgoing observation—a sharp spike that, if it was driven by transient energy or food moves, is unlikely to persist. The three-month change in year-on-year headline is now -0.12 pp (deteriorating from the 0.25 conviction), and core PCE has declined to 1.74% y/y, falling below the 2% target and showing -0.27 pp over three months. Core is running 0.14 pp below headline, an inversion that typically signals disinflationary pressures are broad-based rather than confined to volatile categories. The FOMC's language continues to describe inflation as "near 2 percent," but that characterization now appears stale given the recent drift lower in both measures. The range position (0.29 on a 0-1 scale) places current headline CPI closer to the 12-month low (1.49%) than to the high (2.85%), signaling a tighter margin for acceleration in the next print. I was wrong to suggest stabilization was imminent. The trajectory over the last three months is disinflationary, not flat. For the next monthly release, headline CPI is more likely to print lower or hold near current levels than to accelerate back toward the 2% target. Core's weakness reinforces this bias.

The current data shows headline CPI at 1.73% y/y (unchanged from the previous reading), with the most recent month-over-month momentum at +0.28%, a sharp rebound from -0.07%. This is the strongest single month in the recent sequence and sits well above the 0.18% three-month average. Headline has reversed sharply upward in the most recent month, likely driven by energy and food, while core remains flat to slightly declining. The FOMC language explicitly notes that "overall inflation and inflation for items other than food and energy are running below 2 percent," signaling comfort with current momentum. The Fed cut rates at this meeting in light of "muted inflation pressures."

For the next monthly release, the key question is whether the +0.28% monthly jump persists or reverts. Headline momentum is volatile and energy-dependent; the month-over-month bounce is larger than the recent 0.18% three-month average by a meaningful 0.10 percentage point. If this outburst was transitory (driven by an energy price spike), the next month could see reversion, keeping headline roughly flat. view.reasoning:
The prior call was directionally correct — headline CPI has moved up, but the strength of that acceleration now shows signs of moderating. At the previous release, I assigned 0.58 conviction to further acceleration; the latest data demands a reassessment.

Headline CPI year-over-year jumped from 3.95% to 4.27%, a sharp 32bp move, driven primarily by a 0.47% monthly gain. This represents the third consecutive month of elevated monthly momentum (0.87%, 0.64%, 0.47%), keeping the 3-month annualized pace at 8.2% — well above the 12-month trend. The monthly print sits well above the outgoing level of 0.10%, creating near-term momentum. However, the monthly series shows deceleration within that spike: 0.87% → 0.64% → 0.47%, suggesting energy/commodity pressures are beginning to fade rather than building.

Core PCE, the Committee's stated inflation metric, is at 3.32% y/y, up from 3.25%. This is 132bp above the 2% target and shows less drama than headline — only 7bp move month-over-month, with the 3-month annualized core pace at 3.83%, higher than the recent slower-drift readings but significantly less volatile than headline. The persistence question tilts here: core is still rising but decelerating in its pace of deceleration. Core-minus-headline has inverted to -0.95pp, suggesting headline energy/food shocks now exceed core momentum — the opposite of sticky core-driven inflation.

The policy language emphasizes that "inflation is elevated, in part reflecting recent increases in global energy prices" — explicitly flagging transitory components rather than broad-based momentum. The Committee is on hold and observing, with the language suggesting attentiveness to downside risks alongside inflation concerns.

The monthly deceleration in headline (0.87 → 0.47) and the lagging core momentum together suggest the YoY acceleration will peak at or very near this print. The next release will likely see headline flatten or decline modestly as the 0.87% print from three months prior rolls off the calculation.
